subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will learn about time. You will name the seven days of the week in order, use the words today, tomorrow and yesterday, talk about morning, afternoon and evening, meet the two hands on a clock, and read both o'clock and half past times.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Name the days of the week in order and know a week has 7 days.
Use the words today, tomorrow and yesterday correctly.
Talk about morning, afternoon and evening and what happens in each.
Sort a group of school days and weekend days.
Name the parts of a clock: the face, the numbers, and the two hands.
Tell the hour hand (short) from the minute hand (long).
Read simple o'clock times on a clock.
Read simple half past times on a clock.
Put daily events in order using before and after.

concepts.title: The Days of the Week
concepts.explanation: Start with the seven days and their order. Say the days out loud every single day: ‘Today is Wednesday.’ Point to the day on a calendar or card as you say it. Lay out seven cards, one for each day, in a line from Monday to Sunday, then muddle them up and put them back in order. Singing the days to a tune you know fixes the order in your memory far better than saying them over and over.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Lay out seven cards, one for each day, in a line from Monday to Sunday. Say them together while touching each card. Then muddle the cards and put them back in order. Sing the days-of-the-week song (to a tune you know) again and again — a catchy tune fixes the order in memory far better than plain repeating. Connect days to real events you look forward to: ‘Friday is Jummah — we go to the masjid,’ or ‘Saturday, we visit Grandma.’ Once the order is secure, introduce today, tomorrow and yesterday. These words are tricky because they change meaning every day, so practise them fresh each morning. If today is Monday, tomorrow will be Tuesday and yesterday was Sunday. Keep a finger on the calendar so you can see the movement from one day to the next. Then sort the week into school days (Monday to Friday) and weekend days (Saturday and Sunday). Colour the two groups differently on the calendar so the pattern is easy to see. A gentle note on a common mix-up: in our calendars the week starts on Monday, not Sunday — keep your calendar consistent so you see Monday as the first day every time.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us say the days together. Touch each card. Ready?” You and child: “Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.” You: “Today is Thursday. So what will tomorrow be?” Child: “Friday!” You: “Yes — and Friday is Jummah. What day was yesterday?” Child: “Wednesday.”

concepts.title: Parts of the Day — Morning, Afternoon, Evening
concepts.explanation: There are three easy parts: morning (from waking until lunch), afternoon (from lunch until dinner) and evening (from dinner until bed). You already live this rhythm every day; these are simply its names. Walk through your own day in order: wake for Fajr and eat breakfast in the morning, lunch and play in the afternoon, Maghrib and dinner in the evening. The sun helps too — it comes up in the morning, sits high in the afternoon and goes down in the evening.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Talk through your own day in order. ‘In the morning we wake for Fajr and eat breakfast. In the afternoon we have lunch and play. In the evening we pray Maghrib, eat dinner and get ready for bed.’ Sort picture cards — breakfast, playing after school, a bedtime story — into the three parts. Link the parts to the sun: the sun comes up in the morning, is high in the afternoon, and goes down in the evening. The daily prayers make lovely natural anchors — Fajr in the early morning, Dhuhr in the middle of the day, Maghrib as the sun sets. This is also the perfect place to practise sequencing with the words before and after. Ask, ‘What do we do before we sleep?’ or ‘What comes after breakfast?’ Putting the events of a day in order is the foundation that reading a clock will later sit on.

Before clocks, help the child feel the shape of a day.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Think about our day. What do we do first, in the morning?” Child: “Wake up and pray Fajr, then breakfast.” You: “Well done. Does dinner come before bed, or after bed?” Child: “Before bed!” You: “Yes — dinner in the evening, then we sleep.”

concepts.title: Meeting the Clock — the Two Hands
concepts.explanation: Now bring out a clock. First, just look at it together. Point to the round face, the numbers 1 to 12 going around the edge, and the two hands that move. The single most important idea to fix here is which hand is which: the short hand is the hour hand, and the long hand is the minute hand. Colour helps: make the short hour hand red and the long minute hand blue, and use the same two colours every time so the hands never get muddled.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Use colour to make the hands easy to tell apart — for example, make the short hour hand red and the long minute hand blue, and use the same colours every single time. Point to each hand and say its job: ‘The short hour hand tells us the hour. The long minute hand tells us the minutes.’ A common childhood muddle is thinking the long hand is the hour hand because it looks more important — keep repeating ‘short hand = hour, long hand = minute’ until it is second nature. Move the hands themselves; touching and turning them teaches far more than watching.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Show me the short hand. What is its name?” Child: “The hour hand.” You: “Show me the long hand. What is its name?” Child: “The minute hand.” You: “Short hand tells the hour, long hand tells the minutes. Say it with me.”

concepts.title: Reading O'clock Times
concepts.explanation: Begin with o'clock times only — they are the simplest and should be secure before half past is introduced. The rule is short and clear: when the long minute hand points straight up to 12, we say ‘o'clock’, and the short hour hand tells us which o'clock. Set the clock to 3 o'clock: the long hand is on 12 and the short hand is on 3. Move the short hand round and read each new time. Tying them to your own routine helps — school starts at 9 o'clock, lunch is at 12 o'clock.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Set the clock to 3 o'clock. Say together, ‘The long hand is on 12, the short hand is on 3 — it is 3 o'clock.’ Move the short hand around and read each new o'clock time. Tie times to the routine: ‘School starts at 9 o'clock,’ ‘Lunch is at 12 o'clock.’ Play a quick ‘show me’ game — ‘Show me 5 o'clock on your clock’ — so the child both reads and makes times. Keep the minute hand on 12 the whole time so the only thing that changes is the hour.

concepts.title: Reading Half Past Times
concepts.explanation: Only move to half past once o'clock times are easy and confident. ‘Half past’ means we are halfway through the hour — thirty minutes past. Show ‘half’ with something concrete first: half of a piece of anjero, or half of a paper circle coloured in. Then explain that on a clock, when the long minute hand points down to 6, it is half past.
concepts.example: Expecting the hour hand to sit exactly on a number at half past. Show with a movable clock how the short hand drifts between two numbers as the minutes pass.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Set the clock to half past 7. Point out that the long hand is on 6 (halfway round) and the short hand is between the 7 and the 8. Say, ‘It is half past 7.’ The gradual drift of the short hand is a common stumbling point — children expect it to sit exactly on a number. Show slowly, with a movable clock, how the hour hand creeps from one number towards the next as the minute hand travels round. Read several half past times, always tying them to real moments: ‘We might eat breakfast at half past 7.’ Finally, mix o'clock and half past times so you choose which they are looking at. The single question to ask every time is: ‘Where is the long hand? On 12, it is o'clock. On 6, it is half past.’ This one check unlocks every time in this unit. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Look at the long hand. It is on the 6. Is this o'clock or half past?” Child: “Half past!” You: “Yes. The short hand is between 7 and 8, so it is half past 7. Well done.” Thinking the week starts on Sunday. Keep one consistent calendar that shows Monday as the first day, and always read the days in the same order. Believing the long hand is the hour hand because it looks bigger. Use consistent colours and keep repeating ‘short hand = hour, long hand = minute’.

explorations.title: The Days of the Week
explorations.context: Start with the seven days and their order.
explorations.prompt: What day comes right after Monday?
explorations.hint: Say the days in order starting from Monday: Monday, Tuesday…
explorations.explanation: Say the day out loud every single day rather than learning it once and forgetting — the sequence becomes secure through daily repetition, not through a single explanation.
explorations.grownUpGuide: Singing the order to a familiar tune also helps a pre-reader hold seven items in the right order long before they can read the words.

explorations.title: Parts of the Day — Morning, Afternoon, Evening
explorations.context: There are three easy parts: morning (from waking until lunch), afternoon (from lunch until dinner) and evening (from dinner until bed).
explorations.prompt: Do we usually eat breakfast in the morning or in the evening?
explorations.hint: Think about what you do right after you wake up.
explorations.explanation: Walk through your own day in the order it actually happens, naming each part as you go, so the words attach to what you already do rather than to an abstract idea. Sorting picture cards of daily activities into three piles afterwards checks whether the labels have stuck.
explorations.grownUpGuide: Before clocks, help the child feel the shape of a day.

explorations.title: Meeting the Clock — the Two Hands
explorations.context: Now bring out a clock. First, just look at it together. Point to the round face, the numbers 1 to 12 going around the edge, and the two hands that move.
explorations.prompt: Which hand on a clock is the hour hand — the short one or the long one?
explorations.hint: Remember: short hand tells the hour, long hand tells the minutes.
explorations.explanation: Colour-coding the hands — red for the short hour hand, blue for the long minute hand — and using the same two colours every time removes the guesswork before any time-telling begins.
explorations.grownUpGuide: Get the child comfortable naming ‘short hand’ and ‘long hand’ correctly before introducing the words ‘hour’ and ‘minute’ at all.

explorations.title: Reading O'clock Times
explorations.context: Begin with o'clock times only — they are the simplest and should be secure before half past is introduced. The rule is short and clear: when the long minute hand points straight up to 12, we say ‘o'clock’, and the short hour hand tells us which o'clock.
explorations.prompt: The long hand points to 12 and the short hand points to 5. What time is it?
explorations.hint: When the long hand is on 12, read the hour from the short hand.
explorations.explanation: The one rule to repeat every time is: when the long hand points straight up to 12, read the o'clock time from wherever the short hand is pointing. Tying each o'clock time to something you already do — school, lunch, bedtime — makes the number mean something rather than being just a fact to recall.

explorations.title: Reading Half Past Times
explorations.context: Only move to half past once o'clock times are easy and confident. ‘Half past’ means we are halfway through the hour — thirty minutes past. Show ‘half’ with something concrete first: half of a piece of anjero, or half of a paper circle coloured in.
explorations.prompt: The long hand points to 6 and the short hand is between 2 and 3. What time is it?
explorations.hint: At half past, say the smaller hour number — the one the short hand has already passed.
explorations.explanation: The tricky part is that at half past, the short hand sits between two numbers rather than on one. Say the smaller of the two — the hour that has already passed, not the one it is moving towards. Once both o'clock and half past feel secure, mix the two kinds of times together and ask ‘where is the long hand?’ as the one check every time, so you learn to tell them apart confidently.

explorations.title: The Days of the Week
explorations.context: Start with the seven days and their order.
explorations.prompt: Fill in the missing days: Monday · ______ · Wednesday · ______ · Friday · ______ · Sunday
explorations.hint: Say the days of the week in order to find each gap.
explorations.explanation: When a day is missing from a pattern like this, say the whole sequence from the beginning rather than guessing in isolation — reciting ‘Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday…’ out loud until you reach the gap makes the missing day obvious. This also reinforces that the order never changes, which is the whole point of learning the days as a fixed sequence.

methods.title: Ordering the Days of the Week
methods.example: Example: Say the days in order while touching seven cards laid out from Monday to Sunday.
steps: Lay out seven cards, one for each day, in a line from Monday to Sunday.
Say each day out loud together while touching its card, then mix up the cards and rebuild the line in order.
Point to today's card and say what day comes after it.

methods.title: Using Today, Tomorrow and Yesterday
methods.example: Example: If today is Tuesday, tomorrow is Wednesday and yesterday was Monday.
steps: Each morning, say together, 'Today is ___.'
Ask, 'What was yesterday?' and 'What will tomorrow be?', pointing to the calendar as you answer.
Practise with a new example each day so you hear the words change with the date.

methods.title: Sorting Morning, Afternoon and Evening
methods.example: Example: Sort a picture of breakfast under 'morning' and a picture of Maghrib prayer under 'evening.'
steps: Collect or draw picture cards of daily activities: waking up, lunch, playing, dinner, sleeping.
Sort the cards into three piles: morning, afternoon and evening.
Explain why each card belongs in its pile.

methods.title: Sorting School Days and Weekend Days
methods.example: Example: Sort Monday-to-Friday cards under 'School day' and Saturday and Sunday cards under 'Weekend day.'
steps: Write or draw the seven days on separate cards.
Set up two mats or boxes labelled 'School day' and 'Weekend day.'
Sort each day card into the correct box and say why it belongs there.

methods.title: Naming the Parts of a Clock
methods.example: Example: Point to the clock face, the numbers 1 to 12, and the two hands in turn.
steps: Bring out a real or toy clock and look at it together.
Point to the round face, the numbers going around the edge, and the two hands.
Point to each part when you name it: face, numbers, hour hand, minute hand.

methods.title: Telling the Hour Hand from the Minute Hand
methods.example: Example: Colour the short hour hand red and the long minute hand blue on a paper clock.
steps: Colour the short hand red and the long hand blue on a paper clock.
Ask, 'Which hand is short? Which hand is long?' and name each one together.
Move each hand in turn and say its name before reading the time.

workedExamples.title: Ordering Days of the Week
workedExamples.prompt: Put these days in order: Wednesday, Monday, Friday, Tuesday.
workedExamples.solution: Say the days of the week in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Find where Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday fall in that order. The correct order is Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday.

workedExamples.title: Tomorrow and Yesterday from Thursday
workedExamples.prompt: Today is Thursday. What is tomorrow, and what was yesterday?
workedExamples.solution: Tomorrow is the day after today, so tomorrow is Friday. Yesterday is the day before today, so yesterday was Wednesday.

workedExamples.title: Which Part of the Day is Breakfast?
workedExamples.prompt: Is eating breakfast something we do in the morning or the evening?
workedExamples.solution: We eat breakfast soon after we wake up. Waking up happens in the morning. So breakfast belongs to the morning part of the day.

workedExamples.title: Sorting School Days and Weekend Days
workedExamples.prompt: Sort these into school days and weekend days: Saturday, Monday, Sunday, Wednesday.
workedExamples.solution: School days are Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Weekend days are Saturday and Sunday. So Monday and Wednesday are school days, and Saturday and Sunday are weekend days.

workedExamples.title: Naming the Parts of a Clock
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a clock. What are the round part, the numbers, and the two moving pointers called?
workedExamples.solution: The round part we look at is called the clock face. The numbers 1 to 12 go around its edge. The two moving pointers are called the hour hand and the minute hand.

workedExamples.title: Hour Hand or Minute Hand?
workedExamples.prompt: One hand on the clock is short and one is long. Which is the hour hand and which is the minute hand?
workedExamples.solution: The short hand is the hour hand — it tells us the hour. The long hand is the minute hand — it tells us the minutes. A helpful trick is to colour the short hand red and the long hand blue so they are never mixed up.

workedExamples.title: Reading 6 O'clock
workedExamples.prompt: The long hand points to 12 and the short hand points to 6. What time is it?
workedExamples.solution: When the long hand points to 12, we read an o'clock time. The short hand is on 6, so the time is 6 o'clock.

workedExamples.title: Reading Half Past 8
workedExamples.prompt: The long hand points to 6 and the short hand is between 8 and 9. What time is it?
workedExamples.solution: When the long hand points to 6, it is a half past time. The short hand is between 8 and 9, meaning the hour 8 has just passed. So the time is half past 8.

workedExamples.title: The Day After Wednesday and Before Saturday
workedExamples.prompt: What day comes after Wednesday, and what day comes before Saturday?
workedExamples.solution: Saying the days in order — Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday — shows the day after Wednesday is Thursday. The day before Saturday is Friday.

workedExamples.title: Tomorrow and Yesterday from Tuesday
workedExamples.prompt: If today is Tuesday, what is tomorrow, and what was yesterday?
workedExamples.solution: Tomorrow is the next day, so tomorrow is Wednesday. Yesterday is the day before, so yesterday was Monday.

workedExamples.title: Which Part of the Day is Maghrib and Dinner?
workedExamples.prompt: We pray Maghrib and eat dinner. Which part of the day is this?
workedExamples.solution: Maghrib is prayed after the sun sets, and dinner comes soon after. Sunset and dinner both happen in the evening. So this is the evening part of the day.

workedExamples.title: Is Sunday a School Day?
workedExamples.prompt: Is Sunday a school day or a weekend day?
workedExamples.solution: School days are Monday to Friday. Sunday is not in that list, and it comes right before Monday starts a new week. So Sunday is a weekend day.

practice.prompt: Say the days of the week in order, starting with Monday.
practice.answer: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
practice.hint: Start with Monday and count on your fingers.

practice.prompt: How many days are in one week?
practice.hint: Count the days from Monday to Sunday.

practice.prompt: Name something you do in the morning, something in the afternoon, and something in the evening.
practice.answer: Morning: waking up and eating breakfast. Afternoon: eating lunch and playing. Evening: praying Maghrib and eating dinner.
practice.hint: Think about your own day from waking up to bedtime.

practice.prompt: Amina puts one date on the calendar for each school day this week. How many dates does she put out?
practice.answer: 5 dates, one for each school day (Monday to Friday).
practice.hint: Count only the school days, not the weekend.

practice.prompt: Write the missing days: Monday, Tuesday, ___, Thursday, ___, Saturday, Sunday.
practice.hint: Say the days of the week in order to find the gaps.

practice.prompt: Look at the pattern: Monday, ___, Wednesday, ___, Friday, ___, Sunday. Fill in the missing days.
practice.hint: Say each day out loud in order to spot what is missing.

practice.prompt: Hassan makes a paper clock using a plate and two bottle caps for hands. The long cap points to 12 and the short cap points to 4. What time does his clock show?
practice.hint: The long hand on 12 means it is an o'clock time — read the short hand for the hour.
Say the days in order starting from Wednesday.
Say the days in order and stop just before Saturday.

practice.prompt: If today is Tuesday, tomorrow is ____________.
practice.hint: Tomorrow is the day that comes right after today.

practice.prompt: Fatima's family prays Maghrib, eats dinner and goes to sleep. Is this part of the day the morning, afternoon or evening?
practice.hint: Think about what happens after the sun sets.

practice.prompt: Sort these into school days and weekend days: Sunday, Tuesday, Saturday, Thursday.
practice.answer: School days: Tuesday and Thursday. Weekend days: Sunday and Saturday.
practice.hint: School days are Monday to Friday; the weekend is Saturday and Sunday.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.text: O'clock times are the simplest, so learn them first. The rule is short and clear: when the long minute hand points straight up to 12, we say ‘o'clock’, and the short hour hand tells us which o'clock.

fluency.prompt: Say the day that comes after Friday.
fluency.hint: Think about the day right after Friday, moving toward the weekend.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Sunday', skipping over Saturday. Remember that Saturday comes immediately after Friday.

fluency.prompt: If today is Sunday, what is tomorrow?
fluency.hint: Tomorrow is the day right after today.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Saturday' because it sounds close to Sunday. Remember that a new week starts with Monday right after Sunday.

fluency.prompt: Do we usually go to sleep in the morning or in the evening?
fluency.hint: Think about what happens right before bedtime.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'morning', mixing up waking up with going to sleep. Remember that we wake up in the morning and sleep in the evening.

fluency.prompt: Is Friday a school day or a weekend day?
fluency.hint: School days run from Monday to Friday.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is thinking Friday is already the weekend because it is close to Saturday. Remember that Friday is still a school day.

fluency.prompt: What do we call the round part of the clock that the numbers and hands sit on?
fluency.hint: It's the part you look at to see the whole clock.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is calling it 'the clock hand'. Remember that the hands move, but the round part underneath is called the face.

fluency.prompt: Which hand is longer — the hour hand or the minute hand?
fluency.hint: Look at which hand stretches further across the clock face.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is thinking the hour hand is longer because it moves more slowly. Remember that slow does not mean long — the minute hand is the long one.

fluency.prompt: The long hand is on 12 and the short hand is on 10. What time is it?
fluency.hint: Read the short hand's number when the long hand is on 12.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is reading the wrong hand and saying '12 o'clock'. Remember that for o'clock times, the hour comes from the short hand, not the long one.

fluency.prompt: The long hand is on 6 and the short hand is between 2 and 3. What time is it?
fluency.hint: The short hand tells you which hour has just passed.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'half past 3' by rounding up to the nearer number. Remember that at half past, we name the hour the short hand has already passed, not the one it is approaching.

fluency.prompt: What do we do before we get dressed for school?
fluency.hint: Think about the very start of the school-day routine.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'go to school', which actually comes after getting dressed. Remember to think about what happens earlier in the morning.

fluency.prompt: It is half past 3. Where does the long hand point?
fluency.hint: Remember the rule for half past times.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is pointing to the 3, confusing the short hand's position with the long hand's. Remember that for half past, the long hand always points to 6.

fluency.prompt: Say the day that comes before Monday.
fluency.hint: Think about the very last day of the previous week.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Tuesday', naming the day after Monday instead of before it. Remember that 'before' means earlier, so it is the day the week ends on — Sunday.

fluency.prompt: If today is Saturday, what was yesterday?
fluency.hint: Yesterday is the day right before today.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Sunday', naming tomorrow instead of yesterday. Remember that yesterday looks backward, to the day before.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Amina's mother writes the day on a small board each morning. If she wrote 'Sunday' yesterday, what day should she write today?
realProblems.hint: Think about which day comes right after Sunday.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is answering 'Saturday', confusing yesterday with the day before Sunday instead of the day after it. Remember that today comes after yesterday, so after Sunday comes Monday.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, a vendor sells vegetables every Tuesday and Friday. Today is Tuesday. Will the vendor also be at the market tomorrow?
realProblems.answer: No — tomorrow is Wednesday, and the vendor only sells on Tuesday and Friday.
realProblems.hint: Work out what day tomorrow is first, then check if it matches the vendor's days.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is assuming tomorrow is automatically a market day. Name tomorrow (Wednesday) first, then compare it with the list of market days.

realProblems.prompt: A family leaves for a trip just after sunrise and arrives before lunchtime. Did they travel in the morning or the evening?
realProblems.hint: Think about when the sun rises compared to when the sun sets.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is picking 'evening' because a long trip feels tiring. Remember that sunrise and 'before lunchtime' both belong to the morning, not the evening.

realProblems.prompt: Grandmother places one small stone in a jar for every day of the week, starting from Monday. By the end of Thursday, how many stones are in the jar?
realProblems.answer: 4 stones (for Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday).
realProblems.hint: Count the days from Monday up to and including Thursday.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting only the days before Thursday and forgetting to include Thursday itself, giving 3 instead of 4. Remember that Thursday's own stone is also added.

realProblems.prompt: A family celebration begins on the third day of the week, counting Monday as the first day. Which day is that?
realProblems.hint: Count Monday as day 1, Tuesday as day 2, and keep going.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is counting Monday as day 0, landing on Tuesday instead of Wednesday. Remember to count Monday itself as the first day.

realProblems.prompt: A small shop is closed only on the last day of the week. Which day is the shop closed?
realProblems.hint: Think about which day comes last, from Monday to Sunday.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying 'Saturday', because it sounds like a rest day. Remember that the week runs Monday to Sunday, so Sunday is the true last day.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: If today is Sunday, explain what day tomorrow will be and how you know.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Tomorrow is the day that comes right after today, so I count on one day from Sunday. Since a new week always starts with Monday after Sunday, tomorrow must be Monday. I know this because I say the days of the week in order and Monday always follows Sunday.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how you would find the day that comes after Wednesday.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To find the day after Wednesday, I say the days of the week in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. The day right after Wednesday is Thursday, because 'after' means the next one in the list.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how you would find the day that comes before Saturday.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To find the day before Saturday, I say the days of the week in order and stop just before I reach Saturday: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday. The day right before Saturday is Friday, because 'before' means the one that comes earlier.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading O'clock Times.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: For an o'clock time, the long minute hand always points straight up to 12. Then I look at the short hour hand to see which hour it is. For example, if the long hand is on 12 and the short hand is on 3, the time is 3 o'clock.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading Half Past Times.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: For a half past time, the long minute hand points down to 6, showing that half the hour has gone by. The short hour hand sits between two numbers, and I say the smaller number's hour. For example, if the long hand is on 6 and the short hand is between 7 and 8, the time is half past 7.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in The Days of the Week.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: There are seven days in a week, and they always come in the same order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
